newsitem.title: PERU: Southern Peru earthquake kills seven, injures 500.
newsitem.headline: Southern Peru earthquake kills seven, injures 500.

text.p: A powerful earthquake hit southern Peru on Tuesday, killing seven people and injuring at least 500, officials said.

Officials said they believed earlier reports were false that 300 workers were trapped in an underground mine at the Huanca gold mine, 310 miles (500 km) south of Lima, on the border of the southern departments of Ica and Ayacucho.
"Earlier we had reported 300 trapped but this now appears to have been one of the many false alarms of the day," said Jorge Rodriguez, a police doctor in Ayacucho.

Col. Lucio Corpuera, a civil defence official in Lima, said rescue workers had not arrived at the mine. However, the latest information indicated that only 30 miners were injured in the area in a bus crash after the highway split open.

But Corpuera said it would not be possible to confirm definitively that there were no trapped workers in the mine until around 6 a.m. local time (1100 GMT), when the first helicopters were expected to reach Huanca.
The quake was felt throughout central Peru and shook the capital of Lima for a minute.
Most of the damage was to Nazca, 290 miles (460 km) south of Lima where 300 were injured and nearby Ica, where another 200 were injured, the army said.
The quake caused the collapse of several small mines in the Ica and Ayacucho areas, seriously injuring at least four people, according to local mining unions and rescue workers, Corpuera said.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake measured 7.3 on the open-ended Richter scale and its epicentre was 65 miles (100 km) southeast of Ica.
"It is a major earthquake," said John Minch, a geophysicist at the National Earthquake Information Centre in Golden, Colorado. He said the quake occurred at noon Peru time (1700 GMT).
"It was intense. We had to fly, all of us. The roof of our house practically fell on top of us. There's so much damage," said a devastated Adrian Contreras.
Five of the deaths occurred in Nazca, where 40 percent of the houses suffered serious damage.

Two children and one teenager died from head wounds caused by falling debris, and two men were killed when a landslide demolished homes in one of Nazca's many shantytowns, according to army Gen. Rolando Quezada, who was coordinating rescue work.
A man in neighbouring Ica died of a heart attack brought on by the earthquake, Corpuera said.
In Acari, near Peru's second city, Arequipa, 640 miles (1,030 km) south of Lima, a 60-year old woman died in the quake, Corpuera added without giving details.
In Nazca, medical workers attended to 120 injured people, 40 of whom were still in a serious condition, said Fermin Caceres, director of the Nazca hospital.
"The majority are women, children and elderly who could not run away from the falling walls," Caceres said.
Cira Quispe said people flooded out of their homes, knelt in the streets and prayed for the persistent aftershocks to stop.

Most of the estimated population of 40,000 -- left without light, water or working telephones -- hauled their belongings into the streets and abandoned what was left of their houses in fear of another quake.
"We are going to have to sleep in the street," Quispe said as he waited for the army to fly in blankets and food.
Nazca is one of the main tourist attractions in Peru because of its mysterious pre-Inca lines that form patterns in the desert and can be seen only from the air.
The Andean country is prone to frequent seismic activity. On May 31, 1970, an earthquake measuring 7.8 in magnitude, leveled scores of towns and caused ice and mudslides that killed 67,000 people.
